hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at Fig. 6.1 with switch S at X and trace which plates are joined together - which two capacitors share the same two nodes and so must have the same p.d.?
Hint 2: First add the parallel pair directly, then combine that result in series with the remaining capacitor using the reciprocal rule.
parts.proper_answer: P and T in parallel give $2C$ in series with $C$, so $\frac{1}{C_{total}} = \frac{1}{2C} + \frac{1}{C} = \frac{3}{2C}$, giving $C_{total} = \frac{2}{3}C$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Parallel Pair**
With S at X, the top wire from the middle junction goes to T and the bottom wire of T joins the bottom battery wire, exactly the same two nodes as P. That means P and T are in parallel, so they share the same p.d. and their capacitances simply add. So $$C_{P+T} = C + C = 2C$$

Step 2: **Add the Series Capacitor Q**
This $2C$ combination is in series with Q along the main battery loop, so the charge on Q must equal the charge on the combination. For series we add reciprocals: $$\frac{1}{C_{total}} = \frac{1}{C} + \frac{1}{2C} = \frac{2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2C} = \frac{3}{2C}$$ Flip it over to get $$C_{total} = \frac{2}{3}C$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: the potential difference across capacitor $Q$. Explain your working.

markscheme_points.text: [Answer content not visible in provided image - page rotated/overexposed and cropped; only question label 6(a)(ii) partially visible]

hints: Hint 1: Think of the whole $\frac{2}{3}C$ block across the 9.0 V battery - the total charge moved from the battery must sit on Q because Q is in series with everything else.
Hint 2: Once you have that series charge, use $V = Q/C$ just for capacitor Q alone to find its share of the 9.0 V.
parts.proper_answer: Total charge $Q_{total} = C_{total}V = (2C/3) \times 9.0 = 6.0C$. This is the charge on Q, so $V_Q = Q_{total}/C = 6.0\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Common Series Charge**
The battery sees the combined capacitance, so the charge it supplies is $$Q_{total} = C_{total} \times V = \frac{2}{3}C \times 9.0 = 6.0C$$ In a series line charge cannot pile up anywhere, so this same $6.0C$ must be the charge on Q and the charge on the P+T parallel pair.

Step 2: **Convert Q Charge to Q Voltage**
Now forget the rest of the circuit and focus on Q. It has capacitance $C$ and charge $6.0C$: $$V_Q = \frac{Q_Q}{C_Q} = \frac{6.0C}{C} = 6.0\text{ V}$$ That makes sense because the smaller series capacitor gets the larger share of the voltage. The remaining $3.0\text{ V}$ is across the P+T parallel pair.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Switch $S$ is now moved to position $Y$. State what happens to the potential difference across capacitor $P$ and across capacitor $Q$.

markscheme_points.text: [Answer content not visible in provided image - page rotated/overexposed and cropped; only question label 6(b) partially visible]

hints: Hint 1: With S at Y, redraw the loop in your head - capacitor P is now directly wired across resistor R, forming a discharge loop with no battery in that loop.
Hint 2: Recall what happens to charge on a capacitor when it is left connected only to a resistor - which way does current flow and what is the final p.d.?
Hint 3: Think about steady d.c. conditions after a long time - can any continuous current flow through Q, and so what must the current and p.d. across R be?
Hint 4: Apply conservation of voltage around the battery-Q-P loop once P has reached its final state to deduce the new p.d. across Q.
parts.proper_answer: Capacitor P: p.d. falls to zero as P discharges through R. Capacitor Q: p.d. rises to 9.0 V, the full battery e.m.f., as no current flows in steady state so no p.d. across R and P.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **P Discharges Through R**
Moving S to Y disconnects T and connects R directly across P. P was charged to about $3.0\text{ V}$, so it now drives a current through R. Charge leaves the plates until P is fully discharged. So $$V_P \to 0$$

Step 2: **No Steady Current Can Remain**
Capacitor Q is in series with the battery and the P-R parallel pair. A capacitor blocks steady d.c., so after the transient the current everywhere in that main loop must be zero. With $I = 0$ through R, $$V_R = IR = 0$$

Step 3: **Q Takes the Full Battery Voltage**
Since R and P are in parallel they always share the same p.d., so $V_P = V_R = 0$. Going round the battery loop, Kirchhoff tells us $$9.0 = V_Q + V_P$$ so $$V_Q = 9.0 - 0 = 9.0\text{ V}$$ In words, the p.d. across Q increases from $6.0\text{ V}$ to $9.0\text{ V}$ as extra charge flows onto Q during the discharge transient.
